synthesis_provenance.first_pass_synthesis_verbatim:
I'm researching AI agents, which is annoyingly hard because "agent" gets slapped on anything with a chat box.

The useful version is simpler: it's an AI system that can do more than give you one answer.

It can make decisions, pick tools, read documents, search for information, write things down, call APIs, and work through multiple steps.

So: less "tell me how to plan a trip," more "here are the rules, here are the tools—go figure out the plan."

Which is where it gets interesting.

Because once an AI can interact with information and tools, it can also misunderstand the job, chase the wrong goal, or sound incredibly confident while being completely wrong.

I found the notes from that old workshop-agent experiment. It started small. Then I gave it more context, and suddenly it was making decisions about my projects.

So I think the next question is not, "Is this technically an agent?"

The question is: what should I let it do first?

synthesis_provenance.corrective_pass_synthesis_verbatim:
I'm digging into AI agents, and the annoying part is that everybody uses that phrase like it explains itself.

An agent is not just an AI that gives you one confident paragraph and disappears into the fog. In the useful version, it can make decisions, choose tools, search for information, read documents, write information, call APIs, handle a task with multiple steps, and keep track of what happened along the way.

So instead of asking, "Can AI tell me how to organize a project?" the more interesting question is: can it actually look at the project, find what it needs, use the right tools, and do something useful without wandering into a hedge?

That's where this gets fun. And slightly terrifying in the "why did I give the spreadsheet opinions?" sense.

I found my old workshop-agent notes, from before I gave the thing more context and it started making decisions about my projects. Which is exactly why I'm doing this research carefully. A language model can sound extremely sure while being wrong, misunderstanding the goal, or inventing details with the confidence of a man explaining a parking ticket.

So I'm mapping the boring-but-important bits: what information an agent gets, what tools it can touch, what it remembers, what rules stop it doing something stupid, and how we check its work afterward.

Because "agent" is not the interesting part.

The interesting part is what happens when the AI can actually do something.

If you've got a job you think an agent should try, leave it below.

updated_causal_model.e_knowledge_1_update:
CONFIRMED with a more precise model. Three-layer picture:

(1) Technical KnowledgeDocument determines the available concept SPACE and default vocabulary. This is the lexical reservoir.
(2) An always-present character-invariant communication policy CAN translate SOME of those concepts (state → 'keep track', multi-step → 'multiple steps', system-composition → accessible enumeration).
(3) Some raw source terms may STILL survive when they are (a) the source's canonical name for a concept with no obvious accessible equivalent (e.g. 'call APIs' — the model didn't invent 'connect to other software' this time) or (b) contextually explained rather than translated (e.g. 'language model can sound extremely sure while being wrong').

Slice 6 §96 causal ranking updated: Factor 2 (retrieval omission of communication guidance) is now DIRECTLY confirmed as a load-bearing cause — replacing it with always-present policy measurably reduces at-risk vocabulary while preserving knowledge and identity.
updated_causal_model.architectural_conclusion: YES — the evidence now supports the architectural claim that character-invariant communication behavior should NOT live solely in retrieval-dependent KnowledgeDocuments. When the same rule is always-present in context, output measurably improves on the target dimension while preserving every other dimension.

decision_gate_recommendation.primary: B — Run one replication before promoting the mechanism.
decision_gate_recommendation.reasoning: Trial 4 evidence is directionally strong (2 at-risk vs 5 baseline) and shows both first-pass and corrective-pass shaping. But n=1 for a persona/architectural decision is insufficient. One additional controlled render (Trial 5) — same substrate, same activation — would confirm magnitude stability of the ~2-at-risk residual. If Trial 5 lands in [0, 3] at-risk range with preserved dimensions, Option A (persona migration for Patch) becomes safe. If Trial 5 diverges materially, the interpretation gets richer before any persona edit.
decision_gate_recommendation.alternative: B-variant — replicate under a DIFFERENT topic (still Patch, still nontechnical audience). Same-substrate replication only tests magnitude stability under one retrieval set. Topic-varied replication tests whether the policy generalises to different retrieved chunks. Higher information per render.
decision_gate_recommendation.not_recommended_yet: A (immediate persona migration) — n=1 too low. C (hybrid factual + accessible knowledge rewrite) — architectural conclusion suggests we don't need to rewrite factual knowledge if persona-hosted policy already achieves the result. D (broader Patch/Rivet rewrite) — same reasoning. E (return to Q-270-15c/b) — E-KNOWLEDGE-1 explores a different mechanism (always-present policy) that appears more effective than Q-270-15c revision (Trial 4: 2 at-risk vs Trial 2: 3 at-risk). Continuing corrective-pass work should be de-prioritised behind persona-based fixes.
decision_gate_recommendation.future_direction_if_confirmed: Keep factual technical knowledge intact; move true character invariants to always-present persona/context; only add accessible semantic formulations to factual knowledge IF future evidence shows excessive residual lexical gravity after persona migration. Rivet should eventually receive the same treatment in principle — Slice 6 §100 established the same architectural mechanism operates on Rivet's compression-side failures, even though Rivet's KnowledgeDocument does not currently have a dedicated communication section.
